name: Maya Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the packaging team at Fernhill Creative, which is eight of us in an old warehouse near the canal. Most of our clients are small breweries and bakeries, so my days are can labels, box designs and the odd beer festival poster. Mornings I check my two designers' work and talk to printers about colour proofs. Afternoons I get my own design time, if nobody's label has gone wrong at the printer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part and the worst part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is walking into a bottle shop and seeing a can I designed on the shelf. The worst is when a printer sends back a label and the orange has come out brown, and the brewery's launch is in three days. My partner Theo teaches art at a secondary school, so we both come home with paint or ink on us. I use AI now and then for quick mock-ups, but it's not part of my real process yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures, one by one. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools turned out to be decent assistants and not much more. At work I'd joke that the robots aren't coming for our can labels after all. Online I'd probably say nothing, I don't really post about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel fine about my own job. Breweries want packaging with personality, and they keep coming back because we know their story. Our rent went up last year, but my pay is steady and Fernhill is busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for mock-ups, maybe saving an hour or two a week. I'd keep building savings, we're at about two and a half months now and I want four. I'd push Fernhill's director, Hannah, to finally give my two designers a proper pay rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, maybe, because there's been so much noise about AI and it would end in a shrug. But calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your designers' pay. Why does that matter to you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if AI saves time and the agency keeps all of it, that's not fair. Ruth and Callum are on less than they should be for what they do. If AI saves us two hours a week, my designers should see some of that in their pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else weighing on you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, a bit, like everyone. We're in a one-bedroom and talk about moving somewhere with a spare room for a studio. But that's normal life, not a crisis.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be a **decent assistant** and not much more.
I'd joke at work that the robots aren't coming for our **can labels**.
think: I think my job is **secure**, because breweries come back for our story.
I see **rising rent** as a normal pressure, not a crisis.
do: Keep using AI for **quick mock-ups**, saving an hour or two a week.
Grow savings from **two and a half to four months**.
Push Hannah, the director, for a **pay rise** for her two designers.
feel: She feels **calm** and slightly flat after all the noise.
S0.quote: If AI saves us two hours a week, my designers should see some of that in their pay.
fieldNote: She is **secure** in this world, and her first thought turns to fairness for her team.
She uses AI **casually** and sees no threat from it here.
Rent and wanting a **spare room** are her only steady pressures.

steps.text: Keep designing can labels and boxes for the brewery clients
Grow savings from two and a half to four months
Use AI for quick label mock-ups to save two hours weekly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules on who gets the savings when software does half the work. At Fernhill I'd ask for a team meeting about how we use the tools fairly. Online I'd share stuff from the designers' union about protecting juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my team gets smaller. Mock-ups, layout variations, label copy, resizing for every can size, that's most of what Ruth and Callum do. I'd probably stay, because clients ask for me by name, but I could see Hannah not replacing whoever leaves next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd take a proper short course on AI image and layout tools, so I'm the one setting how we use them. I'd join the union and get Ruth and Callum to join too. I'd move another hundred a month into savings and put off the bigger flat for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into anxious. I'm good at my job and I like it, and I don't want to become a person who just checks machine output. I also feel responsible for my two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ruth and Callum if Hannah said one of their jobs had to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight, before anything was official, if I could. Ruth is better at hand lettering, Callum is faster on production. I'd try to argue for cutting hours across the team instead of cutting one person, even if that meant my hours too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really take fewer hours yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, for a while. Theo and I could manage on less for a year if the flat move waits. Sharing the cut is easier to live with than watching Callum clear his desk.

say: I'd say we need **rules** on who gets the savings when software does the work.
I'd ask Fernhill for a meeting on using the tools **fairly**.
think: I think my **team gets smaller**, since mock-ups and resizing are their main work.
I think I'd stay because clients **ask for me by name**.
do: Take a **short course** on AI image and layout tools this year.
Join the **designers' union** and get Ruth and Callum to join.
Save **another hundred** a month and delay the bigger flat.
feel: She feels **uneasy turning into anxious** about becoming a checker of machine work.
She feels **responsible** for her two designers.
S1.quote: Sharing the cut is easier to live with than watching Callum (her designer) clear his desk.
fieldNote: Her first instinct is **shared sacrifice**, offering to cut her own hours.
She expects her **team to shrink**, which makes her anxious despite her own safety.
She'd learn the tools to **steer** their use, not to replace people.

steps.text: Take a short course on AI layout tools this year
Join the designers' union and bring Ruth and Callum in
Save an extra hundred a month toward four months' cover
Put off moving to a flat with a spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the third picture. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income and shorter working weeks, right now. I'd go to marches with Theo and push the union to do more than write statements. At work I'd say we should be honest with each other about what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Fernhill closes or shrinks to Hannah and one person running the machines. Breweries are small businesses; once a machine can make a good label for almost nothing, they'll take it. The robots coming later doesn't help me, my whole job is on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd sit with Theo and work out a budget on his teaching pay alone. I'd use the two years to grab as much freelance work as possible and save every bit. I'd also look hard at teaching, maybe a teaching qualification in art and design, because classrooms are full of hands-on work and people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. It feels like the ground going from under me just as I got good. And angry that nobody planned for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Teaching is Theo's job. How would it feel to follow him into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weird, honestly. Theo (my partner) would love it, and he'd help me, but I always said I'd never teach. A classroom is a lot of hands-on work and people, and that's what lasts longest here. I'd swallow my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm okay and I have a plan, even if I don't fully. My mum worried when I did a design master's instead of something 'safe'. I'd hate to prove her right.

say: I'd say this is the moment for a **basic income** and shorter weeks.
I'd march with Theo and push the **union** to act, not just write statements.
think: I think **Fernhill closes** or shrinks to one person running the machines.
I think the **robot delay** doesn't help, since my whole job is on screen.
do: Budget on **Theo's teaching pay** alone within the first month.
Take **every freelance job** possible in the two years and save it.
Look into a **teaching qualification** in art and design.
feel: She feels properly **scared** that the ground is going just as she got good.
She feels **angry** that nobody planned for this.
S2.quote: My mum worried when I did a design master's instead of something 'safe'. I'd hate to prove her right.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job**, and turns to teaching despite saying she never would.
Her household leans on **Theo's teaching**, a job with more hands-on time.
She worries about **proving her mum right** as much as about money.

steps.text: March with Theo and press the union for basic income
Take every freelance packaging job going for two years
Apply for a teaching qualification in art and design
Bank all freelance earnings on top of her savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if we start now, so let's start now. I'd be the annoying one at union meetings asking what the actual plan is. At work I'd want Hannah to tell clients we're a human studio, and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I get maybe four good years left in design. That's enough to save properly and test whether teaching suits me, without jumping at once. I still think the job goes, it's just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start volunteering one afternoon a month at Theo's school's art club to see if I'd actually like teaching. I'd get savings up to six months by 2029. I'd keep learning the AI tools so I'm the last person Fernhill would let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's less like a cliff and more like a steep hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools to be the last person let go. Does that sit well with your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not entirely, no. It feels a bit like climbing over people. But Hannah won't keep everyone, and I'd rather be there arguing for the others than gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change about your plans with Theo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about kids. We've said maybe at thirty, but I'd want us to wait until we know if I'm teaching or not. I'd hate to be pregnant the year my job disappears.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to plan if we start now.
I'd keep asking the union what the **actual plan** is.
think: I think I have **four good years** left in design.
I think there's time to **test teaching** without jumping at once.
do: Volunteer **one afternoon a month** at the school art club.
Keep learning **AI tools** to stay last on the cut list.
feel: She feels **anxious but with a plan**, more a steep hill than a cliff.
S3.quote: I'd hate to be pregnant the year my job disappears.
fieldNote: She admits learning the tools to stay feels like **climbing over people**.
The timing of **children** now depends on her career change.
Five years turns teaching into a **test run**, not a leap.

steps.text: Volunteer one afternoon a month at the school art club
Build savings to six months of expenses by 2029
Learn Fernhill's AI layout tools deeply this year
Hold off on children until her next job is settled

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, if we use it to share the gains instead of fighting over scraps. I'd back policies for retraining and shorter weeks. At work I'd say let's enjoy the craft while we have it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd stay in design most of that decade. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, and I could finish a teaching qualification part time well before then. The end point still scares me, but it's far enough off to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the packaging team and use AI where it saves the boring bits. Around year five I'd start a part-time teaching qualification. I'd keep saving and have a kid in the middle of the decade if things look steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. I can picture a life on the other side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think the industry looks like by year eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer studios, I think, and the ones left will sell the human part, like a craft brewery sells the brewer. Fernhill might be one of them if Hannah is smart. I'd want to be there for that, then go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The design students graduating in five years, honestly. Design students graduating in five years would be stepping onto a ladder with no bottom rungs. I'd want to teach them, if anything.

I'd back **retraining and shorter weeks** in politics.
think: I think I'd stay in **design most of the decade**.
I think I can finish a **teaching qualification** part time before it lands.
do: Keep leading the **packaging team**, using AI for boring tasks.
Start a **part-time teaching** qualification around year five.
Keep saving and plan a **child mid-decade** if things look steady.
feel: She feels **uneasy but okay**, and can picture life on the other side.
S4.quote: Design students graduating in five years would be stepping onto a ladder with no bottom rungs.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **stay in design** and plan the switch calmly.
She worries for **graduates** more than for herself.

steps.text: Keep leading Fernhill's packaging team through the decade
Start a part-time teaching qualification around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's too fast for me to retrain or for Theo and me to plan anything. What would help is a guaranteed income while you retrain, and funded teaching places for people switching careers. And rules that make companies share what they save.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people in the middle, like team leads. We're the ones who'd have to tell our designers they're going. Nobody trains you for telling a friend their job is gone.

headlineQuote: Nobody trains you for telling a friend their job is gone.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old team lead** for packaging at Fernhill, designing labels for breweries and bakeries.
She uses AI **now and then** and lives with Theo, a secondary school art teacher.
Her politics show in her **fairness instinct**: share savings, share cuts, protect juniors.
Faced with AGI, she turns toward **teaching**, and she ties plans for children to that switch.
She is calm in the plateau, **alarmed** at two years, and uneasy with ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to retrain or plan with Theo.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** during retraining and funded teaching places.
Rules that make companies **share their savings** with workers.
